title: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis Mimicking Limbic Encephalitis
case_prompt:
A 72-year-old Japanese man with a history of periodontal disease and benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with acute disturbance of consciousness. He was febrile to 38.2°C, agitated, and responded with incoherent speech. His Glasgow Coma Scale score was E4V4M6. Neurological examination showed cerebellar ataxia, sensory aphasia, and bilateral asterixis; there were no meningeal signs.

Laboratory studies revealed blood urea nitrogen 88.2 mg/dL, creatinine 2.09 mg/dL, and D-dimer 7.6 mg/L; other coagulation parameters were normal. Noncontrast head CT and brain MRI showed no hemorrhage, infarction, or focal lesions. Lumbar puncture demonstrated opening pressure of 26 cmH2O; CSF analysis revealed 88 leukocytes/mm3 (85 mononuclear), protein 105 mg/dL, and glucose 76 mg/dL (serum 132 mg/dL).

Given the acute febrile encephalopathy, sensory aphasia, and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, empirical intravenous acyclovir was started for presumed herpes simplex encephalitis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Herpes simplex encephalitis was considered because of acute fever, encephalopathy, and CSF pleocytosis — “the patient was initially suspected of having HSVE based on clinical symptoms and CSF findings, and acyclovir…was initiated.”  
2. Cerebral venous thrombosis was diagnosed when subtle imaging changes were recognized — “before the patient’s admission, a radiologist pointed out cerebral venous thrombosis at the straight and superior sagittal sinuses on brain CT and MRI.”  
3. Hypercoagulable disorders were excluded by laboratory testing — “screening results for anti-double stranded-DNA, lupus anti-coagulant, anti-cardiolipin, anti-nuclear, perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic, and cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were all negative.”  
4. Lemierre’s syndrome was ruled out by ENT evaluation — “otolaryngologists denied an oropharyngeal infection in our case, ruling out Lemierre’s syndrome.”  
5. Infective endocarditis was excluded by echocardiography — “Transthoracic echocardiography also showed no evidence of endocarditis.”  
6. Periodontal Eikenella corrodens bacteremia was identified as the thrombotic source — “blood cultures were positive for Eikenella corrodens … dentists have also pointed out that severe dental caries and gingivitis can be the source of E. corrodens infection.”
